title: Memory & Context

techniques.name: Context Budgeting
techniques.q: What earns a place in the window?
techniques.what: Treat the context window as a scarce attention budget: fill it with the smallest set of high-signal tokens that gets the task done. Decide what enters, in what order and how much, because accuracy falls as input grows, even on simple tasks, and facts buried in the middle of a long prompt are the ones most often missed.
use: Agents that stuff whole documents, clause libraries or tool catalogues into every call
Quality that drops late in long sessions or on long inputs
Teams tempted to buy a bigger window instead of curating
metrics: accuracy changes with input length even on simple tasks (Chroma, 18 models)
facts at the start or end are used best; the middle worst
in RULER only about half of models claiming 32k+ held up at 32k
long documents first, question last: up to 30% better in Anthropic’s tests
pass IDs and let tools fetch full text only when needed
accuracy at your real input lengths, per token spent
steps: Count tokens per segment: system prompt, documents, history, tool results
Find your effective budget: the length where your own eval stays accurate
Rank chunks by relevance and keep the top ones until the budget is spent
Put documents first and the question last; re-run the eval at 8k, 32k and 128k
pitfalls: Trusting the advertised maximum instead of measuring where accuracy falls
Leaving near-duplicate or outdated chunks in as distractors
Burying the most relevant chunk in the middle of a long prompt
techniques.remember: Fewer, better tokens. Key facts at the edges.
techniques.cap: Illustrative accuracies for one contract question. The pattern, not the exact numbers, is what the research shows.

cmp.needs: Token counts and a length eval
cmp.best: Cutting a chunk that was needed

techniques.name: Short-Term Memory and Compaction
techniques.q: How does the agent keep the thread?
techniques.what: Short-term memory is the working state of one session: messages, tool results and plans. When it outgrows the window, the agent clears stale tool results, compacts old turns into a summary, or writes progress notes, while keeping identifiers, amounts, decisions and open tasks intact.
use: Sessions that run for dozens or hundreds of turns
Agents whose tool results (search pages, statements, logs) are large
Tasks that must survive a restart or a context limit
metrics: drop old tool outputs, keep the last few (Claude: keep 3 by default)
summarize old turns into one block (Claude: triggers at 150k by default)
say what must survive: IDs, amounts, dates, decisions, open tasks
a file or row the agent re-reads after each compaction
persist thread state by session ID (LangGraph, Agents SDK Sessions)
each clear rewrites the prefix; clear fewer, larger chunks
steps: Persist the thread by session ID and log input tokens per turn
Clear stale tool results past a trigger, keeping the last few and protecting still-needed tools
Compact old turns with instructions that keep IDs, amounts, decisions and open tasks
Quiz the agent on early-session facts after each compaction
pitfalls: A summary that paraphrases account numbers or amounts
Dropping the first message, which holds the task and constraints
Clearing a little on every turn, which invalidates the prompt cache each time
techniques.remember: Clear the bulk, summarize the rest, keep the IDs.
techniques.cap: Illustrative session: 4.5k tokens a turn. Clearing at 60k plus compaction keeps context under 70k for 120 turns.

cmp.needs: Session store and a summary prompt

techniques.name: Semantic Memory
techniques.q: What does the agent know about this user?
techniques.what: Durable facts about users and entities, stored outside the model and carried across sessions. A pipeline extracts candidate facts from each exchange, reconciles them with what is already stored, and retrieves the relevant few on each turn. The hard part is not storing facts but updating and scoping them.
use: Assistants that serve the same customer across weeks or months
Preferences, goals and profile facts the user should not have to repeat
Replacing long transcript replays with a few retrieved facts
metrics: compare each new fact with similar ones: ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or no-op (Mem0)
one profile document per user, or a collection of small facts
namespace by tenant and user; never search across users
keep validity windows and invalidate contradicted facts (Graphiti)
Mem0 reported over 90% fewer tokens than full context on LOCOMO
updates, multi-session and temporal questions, and abstention (LongMemEval)
steps: Choose the shape: a profile document or a collection of small facts
Extract candidate facts after each exchange
Reconcile each against its most similar stored facts: add, update, delete or skip
Retrieve the top few, scoped to the user, and test updates and abstention
pitfalls: Append-only stores that keep both the old and the new city
A search without the user ID in the namespace, leaking facts between users
Evaluating recall only, never updates or “I don’t know”
techniques.remember: Update, don’t append. Scope every search.
techniques.cap: Illustrative token counts for an investor with five stored facts.

techniques.name: Episodic Memory
techniques.q: Has the agent been here before?
techniques.what: Records of specific past experiences, such as a run, its steps, outcome and time, retrieved when a similar situation arises. Retrieval scores each episode on recency, importance and relevance. Reflection condenses related episodes into short lessons, such as “PAN lookup timed out last time; retry once, then escalate”.
use: Agents that repeat the same mistakes across runs
Operations and support work where past incidents predict fixes
Few-shot examples chosen from the agent’s own successful runs
metrics: exponential decay: 0.995 per hour in Generative Agents
rated 1–10 when the episode is written
cosine similarity between the situation and the episode
min-max normalize each, then weight and add
when recent importance passes a threshold (150), write lessons citing episodes
steps: Log each run as an episode: task, steps, outcome, time and cost
Rate importance when writing; embed the task for relevance
Retrieve by normalized recency, importance and relevance
Reflect into short, cited lessons and inject those instead of transcripts
pitfalls: Adding raw scores, so importance on 1–10 swamps relevance on 0–1
Recency weighted so high that trivial recent events always win
Injecting whole transcripts instead of the lesson they teach
techniques.remember: Normalize the three scores. Inject lessons, not logs.
techniques.cap: Illustrative scores, min-max normalized across the three episodes shown, equal weights.

techniques.name: Write and Forget Policies
techniques.q: What should be saved, and when must it go?
techniques.what: Rules for what becomes memory, how duplicates and conflicts are merged, and when memories expire. Forgetting covers decay, time-to-live limits and user deletion, which must reach every copy: database rows, vectors, summaries and caches. Under India’s DPDP Act, erasure on request or when the purpose ends is a legal duty.
use: Any long-term memory that holds personal data
Regulated sectors: banking, insurance, healthcare
Stores that grow without limit or keep contradicting themselves
metrics: only named categories are saved: preferences, contact channel, goals
never store OTPs, card numbers, Aadhaar, PAN or health data in memory
newer wins; older is invalidated with a date, not silently kept
one-off items expire; unused items fade
delete rows, vectors, summaries and caches; log that it happened
write immediately (latency) or in a scheduled job (cheaper)
DPDP Act right to erasure: remove the person from rows, vectors, summaries, caches and backups on a schedule, then confirm
steps: Allow-list categories and block sensitive patterns before anything is written
Save only stable, reusable facts; skip one-off remarks
Consolidate conflicts and attach a time-to-live per category
Delete everywhere on request, log it, and audit a sample weekly
pitfalls: Deleting database rows but leaving embeddings and summaries behind
Storing OTPs or identity numbers because they appeared in a chat
Keeping both the old and new address with no validity dates
Treating erasure as a one-off script instead of a tested job with a deletion log that holds IDs, not the data
techniques.remember: Save less. Delete everywhere. Keep the proof.
techniques.cap: Illustrative. Legal points are summaries of the DPDP Act and Rules, not legal advice.

cmp.needs: Policy, filters, deletion jobs, audit log

techniques.name: Agent-Managed Memory
techniques.q: Should the agent decide what to remember?
techniques.what: Give the agent tools to view, write, search and edit its own memory, and let it decide when to use them. MemGPT framed this as an operating system paging data between a small main context and larger stores. The agent can then resume long tasks across sessions, but every path and write must be checked.
use: Multi-day tasks that must resume where they stopped
Agents whose useful notes are hard to predict in advance
Workflows where the agent keeps checklists or progress files
metrics: memory_20250818: view, create, str_replace, insert, delete, rename
client-side under /memories: you implement the handlers
resolve every path and check it stays inside the memory root
memory blocks in context plus archival memory the agent searches
memory tool plus context editing: 39% better than baseline in Anthropic’s eval
log every write; sample and review them
steps: Declare the memory tool and implement its handlers on your storage
Resolve each path and reject anything outside the memory root
Let the agent view memory first and record progress as it works
Pair with context editing, and log and review every write
pitfalls: Checking the path with startswith, so /memories/../ escapes
The agent writing sensitive data or instructions into its own memory
Progress written too rarely, so work is redone after a reset
techniques.remember: Let it take notes. Check every path.

techniques.name: Procedural Memory
techniques.q: Has the agent done this kind of task before?
techniques.what: Procedural memory stores how to do things: workflows, checklists, scripts and skills distilled from past successful runs. Instead of rediscovering a multi-step routine every time, the agent retrieves a proven procedure and follows or adapts it, which cuts steps, tokens and errors. It applies to support playbooks and back-office routines as much as to code; research such as Voyager’s skill library and Agent Workflow Memory showed large gains from reusing learned routines.
use: Routines the agent repeats: a KYC re-verification, a refund investigation, adding an API endpoint
Team conventions the agent keeps getting wrong
Long workflows with a stable sequence of tool calls
metrics: facts about the codebase or domain
named, tested code the agent can call
repo-level guides such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md
steps: Log successful trajectories along with the task that triggered them
Distill repeated ones into reusable procedures or scripts, with tests
Index procedures by task description so the agent can retrieve them
Revise or retire procedures when the codebase changes
pitfalls: Stale procedures replay outdated steps with confidence
Retrieving the wrong procedure sends the agent the wrong way
Unreviewed memories can store mistakes or unsafe shortcuts
techniques.cap: The second run skips exploration because the working procedure was saved.

techniques.name: Graph and Temporal Memory
techniques.q: Can the agent remember who is linked to what, and since when?
techniques.what: Stores memory as entities and relationships with time on every edge: who holds which account, who is nominee, which address was valid from when to when. New facts that contradict old ones close the old edge with an end date instead of deleting it, so the agent answers from what is true now and can still explain what was true then. Multi-hop questions follow edges, which plain vector memory struggles to do.
use: Customer relationships that change: nominees, addresses, authorised signatories
Questions that chain facts: “the nominee on the account opened after the move”
Audit needs: what did we know, and when
metrics: typed edges such as holder_of, nominee_of, lives_at
when the fact was true in the world
contradicted edges get an end date
graph traversal plus text and vector search
steps: Extract entities and relationships from each conversation or note
Attach valid-from and valid-to times, and when the fact was recorded
Close contradicted edges instead of deleting them
Answer by traversing the graph for the current time, with vector search for fuzzy matches
pitfalls: Deleting old facts and losing the audit trail
Keeping contradictory facts with no dates, so answers flip
Extraction errors creating wrong edges that nobody reviews
techniques.remember: Link the facts, date the links, close old ones.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Kaveri Bank, a fictional bank, gives relationship managers memory across three years of customer notes.

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-5"                      # use your current model

def n_tokens(text: str) -> int:                                        #@1
    msg = [{"role": "user", "content": text}]                         #@1
    return client.messages.count_tokens(model=MODEL, messages=msg).input_tokens   #@1

inventory = {name: n_tokens(t) for name, t in segments.items()}        #@1
BUDGET = 16_000      # where our own eval stays accurate, not 200_000  #@2

def curate(question, chunks):                                          #@3
    ranked = sorted(chunks, key=lambda c: c.score, reverse=True)       #@3
    kept, used = [], n_tokens(question)                                #@3
    for c in ranked:                                                   #@3
        if used + c.tokens > BUDGET:                                   #@3
            break                                                      #@3
        kept.append(c); used += c.tokens                               #@3
    return kept

index = "\n".join(f"{c.id}: {c.title}" for c in all_clauses)          #@5
TOOLS = [{"name": "get_clause", "description": "Fetch one clause by ID",   #@5
          "input_schema": {"type": "object",                            #@5
                           "properties": {"id": {"type": "string"}}}}]  #@5

for length in (8_000, 32_000, 128_000):                                #@6
    print(length, run_eval(EVAL_SET, pad_to=length))                   #@6
steps: Inventory the window
Count tokens per segment before sending. Here the clause library takes 90k of a 123k prompt; the system prompt, history and tools take the rest.
Set an effective budget
The advertised window is 200k, but your own eval stays accurate only up to about 16k on this task. That measured length is the budget.
Rank by signal
Score every chunk against the question and keep the top ones until the budget is spent. Five clauses, about 7.5k tokens, carry the answer.
Order deliberately
Documents go first, most relevant at the top, and the question goes last. Nothing critical sits in the middle of a long block.
Load just in time
Instead of full text for all 60 clauses, pass a short index of IDs and titles, and a get_clause tool the agent calls when it needs one.
Re-test at length
Run the same eval with inputs padded to 8k, 32k and 128k. The drop at 128k is why the budget exists; re-check it when models change.

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
store = SessionStore("redis://localhost:6379")        # your own store      #@1

EDITS = [
  {"type": "clear_tool_uses_20250919",                                    #@3
   "trigger": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 60_000},                  #@3
   "keep": {"type": "tool_uses", "value": 3},                             #@3
   "clear_at_least": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 20_000},           #@3
   "exclude_tools": ["get_loan_summary"]},                                #@3
  {"type": "compact_20260112",                                            #@4
   "trigger": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 120_000},                 #@4
   "instructions": "Summarize the call. Copy verbatim: loan account, "    #@4
       "agreed EMI, NEFT mandate status, decisions and open tasks."}]     #@4

def turn(session_id, user_text):
    msgs = store.get(session_id) or [TASK_MESSAGE]                        #@1
    msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
    r = client.beta.messages.create(
        model=MODEL, max_tokens=2048, tools=TOOLS, messages=msgs,
        betas=["context-management-2025-06-27", "compact-2026-01-12"],    #@3,4
        context_management={"edits": EDITS})                              #@3,4
    metrics.log(session_id, input_tokens=r.usage.input_tokens)            #@2
    msgs.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})  # keeps compaction   #@1,4
    if any(b.type == "compaction" for b in r.content):                    #@5
        msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": read_note(session_id)})   #@5
    store.set(session_id, msgs)                                           #@1
    return r

PROBES = {"Loan account?": "HL-4471093", "Agreed EMI?": "18,400"}          #@6
def survived(session_id):                                                  #@6
    return {q: a in ask(session_id, q) for q, a in PROBES.items()}        #@6
steps: Persist the thread
Store the messages by session ID so a two-hour call survives restarts. The first message holds the task and constraints; it stays pinned.
Measure growth
Log input tokens every turn. Each turn adds about 1k of talk and a 3.5k statement or schedule, so the context passes 150k by turn 33.
Clear stale tool results
Past the trigger, old tool results are replaced by placeholders; the last 3 stay, and get_loan_summary is excluded because the agent still refers to it.
Compact with instructions
When the conversation itself grows too long, older turns become one summary. The instructions say what must be copied exactly.
Keep a progress note
After a compaction the agent re-reads a short note of decisions and open tasks, so work carries on from the right place.
Check what survived
Probe the agent with questions about early turns. If the loan account or EMI is wrong, fix the instructions before shipping.

from mem0 import Memory
m = Memory.from_config(CONFIG)          # your LLM + vector store         #@1
# collection: many small facts per investor (a profile is one document) #@1

def remember(tenant, investor, user_msg, reply):
    out = m.add([{"role": "user", "content": user_msg},                  #@2
                 {"role": "assistant", "content": reply}],               #@2
                user_id=f"{tenant}:{investor}")                          #@2,4
    for ev in out["results"]:            # ADD / UPDATE / DELETE / NONE   #@3
        log.info("%s %s", ev["event"], ev["memory"])                      #@3

def recall(tenant, investor, question, k=3):
    hits = m.search(question, user_id=f"{tenant}:{investor}", limit=k)   #@4,5
    return "\n".join(f"- {h['memory']}" for h in hits["results"])      #@5

def system_prompt(tenant, investor, question):
    facts = recall(tenant, investor, question)                           #@5
    return f"{RULES}\n<investor_facts>\n{facts}\n</investor_facts>"   #@5

CASES = [("Where does the investor live?", "Bengaluru"),   # changed     #@6
         ("Monthly SIP amount?", "8,000"),                 # updated     #@6
         ("Investor's employer?", "don't know")]           # never said  #@6
score = sum(exp.lower() in answer(q).lower() for q, exp in CASES) / len(CASES)   #@6
steps: Choose profile or collection
A profile is one document per investor, rewritten as facts change. A collection keeps many small facts and retrieves a few. Here: a collection.
Extract facts per exchange
After each exchange an LLM pulls out candidate facts: “lives in Pune”, “prefers Hindi”, “SIP ₹5,000 a month”.
Reconcile with the store
Each candidate is compared with the most similar stored facts. “We moved to Bengaluru” becomes an UPDATE, not a second city.
Scope by tenant and user
Every write and search carries the tenant and investor ID, so one investor’s facts can never be retrieved for another.
Retrieve top-k per turn
The few most relevant facts go near the top of the system prompt: about 180 tokens instead of 26k of old transcripts.
Evaluate updates and abstention
Test questions whose answer changed and questions the investor never answered. “I don’t know” is the right answer to the last one.

import time, numpy as np
episodes, lessons, since_reflect = [], [], 0

def log_episode(task, steps, outcome, cost):                              #@1
    ep = dict(id=len(episodes), task=task, steps=steps, outcome=outcome,  #@1
              cost=cost, hour=time.time() / 3600, vec=embed(task))        #@1
    ep["importance"] = int(llm("Rate 1-10 how important this is "         #@2
                               f"to remember. Reply with a number.\n{outcome}"))   #@2
    episodes.append(ep); reflect_if_needed(ep["importance"])              #@1,4

def norm(x):                                                              #@3
    x = np.asarray(x, float); return (x - x.min()) / (x.max() - x.min() + 1e-9)   #@3

def retrieve(query, k=3):                                                 #@3
    now, q = time.time() / 3600, embed(query)                             #@3
    rec = norm([0.995 ** (now - e["hour"]) for e in episodes])            #@3
    imp = norm([e["importance"] for e in episodes])                       #@3
    rel = norm([float(np.dot(q, e["vec"])) for e in episodes])            #@3
    return [episodes[i] for i in np.argsort(-(rec + imp + rel))[:k]]      #@3

def reflect_if_needed(importance, threshold=150):                         #@4
    global since_reflect; since_reflect += importance                     #@4
    if since_reflect >= threshold:                                        #@4
        lessons.append(llm("Write short lessons, citing episode ids:\n"  #@4
                           + summarize(episodes[-30:])))                  #@4
        since_reflect = 0                                                 #@4

def context_for(query):                                                   #@5
    return "\n".join(relevant_lessons(lessons, query, k=2))   # not transcripts   #@5

repeat_rate = repeated_errors(last_week) / len(last_week)                 #@6
steps: Log episodes
Each run becomes a record: task, steps, outcome, time and cost. A PAN lookup that timed out three weeks ago is one episode among thousands.
Score importance
When writing, an LLM rates importance from 1 to 10. A failed lookup that kept a customer waiting scores 8; “customer said thanks” scores 1.
Retrieve by three scores
Recency decays by 0.995 per hour, importance comes from the rating, relevance from embedding similarity. Each is min-max normalized, then added.
Reflect past a threshold
When the importance of new episodes adds up to 150, the agent writes short lessons that cite the episodes they came from.
Inject lessons, not transcripts
The prompt gets “PAN API times out at month-end; retry once, then escalate”, 40 tokens, instead of five past transcripts.
Measure repeat errors
Track how often the agent repeats a mistake it has seen before. That rate, not recall, shows whether episodic memory works.

import re, datetime as dt
ALLOW = {"language", "channel", "goal", "address", "complaint"}            #@1
BLOCK = [r"\bOTP\b", r"\b[A-Z]{5}\d{4}[A-Z]\b",        # OTPs, PAN     #@1
         r"\b\d{4}\s?\d{4}\s?\d{4}\b", r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,16}\b"]   # Aadhaar, cards   #@1
TTL = {"complaint": dt.timedelta(days=30)}                # one-offs expire   #@4

def write(uid, c):                     # c: category, text, stability 0-1
    if c.category not in ALLOW or any(re.search(p, c.text, re.I) for p in BLOCK):   #@1
        return "blocked"                                                   #@1
    if c.stability < 0.7:              # a remark, not a reusable fact     #@2
        return "skipped"                                                   #@2
    now = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc)
    for old in db.find(uid, category=c.category, valid=True):             #@3
        db.update(old.id, valid=False, invalid_at=now)    # newer wins     #@3
    expires = now + TTL[c.category] if c.category in TTL else None        #@4
    row = db.insert(uid, c, valid=True, created=now, expires=expires)     #@3,4
    vectors.upsert(row.id, embed(c.text), {"user": uid})                  #@3

def erase(uid):                                                           #@5
    rows = db.delete(user=uid); vecs = vectors.delete(filter={"user": uid})   #@5
    summaries.delete(uid); cache.delete(f"profile:{uid}")                 #@5
    audit.append({"event": "erasure", "user": uid, "rows": rows,          #@5
                  "vectors": vecs, "at": dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc)})   #@5

def weekly_audit(n=200):                                                  #@6
    bad = [r for r in db.sample(n) if any(re.search(p, r.text, re.I) for p in BLOCK)]   #@6
    return len(bad), expired_but_present(), deletions_without_audit()     #@6
steps: Allow-list and block
Only named categories may be written, and patterns for OTPs, PAN, Aadhaar and card numbers are blocked before anything reaches a store.
Save stable facts only
“Prefers Hindi” is reusable; “asked the gold rate today” is not. A stability score below 0.7 means skip.
Consolidate conflicts
A new address invalidates the old one with a date instead of sitting beside it. History stays for audit; retrieval sees only valid facts.
Attach TTLs
One-off complaints expire after 30 days. Unused items can also decay, so the store does not grow forever.
Delete everywhere
An erasure removes rows, vectors, rolling summaries and caches. One audit line records that it happened, without the data.

import anthropic, logging
from pathlib import Path
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
ROOT = Path("memories").resolve()
TOOLS = [{"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}]                    #@1

def safe(p: str) -> Path:                                                 #@3
    full = (ROOT / p.removeprefix("/memories").lstrip("/")).resolve()     #@3
    if not full.is_relative_to(ROOT):                                     #@3
        raise PermissionError(f"outside /memories: {p}")                  #@3
    return full                                                           #@3

def run_memory(cmd: dict) -> str:                                         #@2
    path = safe(cmd["path"])                                              #@2,3
    if cmd["command"] == "view":                                          #@2
        return "\n".join(x.name for x in path.iterdir()) if path.is_dir() else path.read_text()   #@2
    if cmd["command"] == "create":                                        #@2
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True); path.write_text(cmd["file_text"])   #@2
    # str_replace, insert, delete, rename (old_path/new_path) follow the same pattern
    logging.info("memory %s %s", cmd["command"], path)                    #@6
    return "ok"

msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": "Continue the ITR checklist for client 114."}]   #@4
while True:
    r = client.beta.messages.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=2048,
        tools=TOOLS, messages=msgs,                                        #@4
        betas=["context-management-2025-06-27"],                          #@5
        context_management={"edits": [{"type": "clear_tool_uses_20250919"}]})   #@5
    msgs.append({"role": "assistant", "content": r.content})
    calls = [b for b in r.content if b.type == "tool_use"]                #@4
    if not calls:                                                         #@4
        break                                                             #@4
    msgs.append({"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "tool_result",      #@4
        "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": run_memory(b.input)} for b in calls]})   #@4
steps: Declare the memory tool
memory_20250818 is a client-side tool. Claude sends view, create, str_replace, insert, delete and rename commands; your code stores the files.
Implement the handlers
Map each command onto your own storage: a folder, a database or object storage, per tenant and client.
Validate every path
Resolve the path first, then check it is still inside the memory root. /memories/../config.env resolves outside and is refused.
Run the loop
The agent views its memory first, finds progress.md at item 12 of 30, resumes at 13 and updates the file as it goes.
Pair with context editing
Clearing old tool results keeps each session small. Before results are cleared, the agent can save what matters to memory.
Log and review writes
Every write is logged with its path, so a person can review what the agent chose to remember.

LOG = []                                                     #@1
def record(task, steps, tests_passed):                       #@1
    if tests_passed:                  # keep only verified runs  #@1
        LOG.append({"kind": task.kind, "steps": steps})      #@1

def distill(kind, min_runs=3):                               #@2
    runs = [r for r in LOG if r["kind"] == kind]             #@2
    if len(runs) < min_runs:                                 #@2
        return None                                          #@2
    best = min(runs, key=lambda r: len(r["steps"]))          #@2
    return Skill(name=kind, steps=best["steps"], check="make test")   #@2

skill = distill("add_api_endpoint")                          #@2,3
store.add(text=skill.description, item=skill,                #@3
          meta={"commit": git_head(), "failures": 0})        #@3

hit = store.search(new_task.text, k=1)[0]                    #@4
if hit.score >= 0.80:                                        #@4
    plan = hit.item.steps                  # reuse the skill #@4
else:
    plan = agent.explore(new_task)         # no match: explore   #@4

agent.follow(plan)                                           #@5
if run(skill.check) != 0:                  # verify every reuse  #@5,6
    hit.meta["failures"] += 1                                #@6
    if hit.meta["failures"] >= 2:                            #@6
        store.retire(skill.name)           # stale after a refactor  #@6
steps: Log verified runs
Record each successful trajectory with the kind of task it solved. Only runs whose tests passed are kept, so mistakes are not memorized.
Distill a repeated routine
After three runs of the same kind, keep the shortest one as a named skill: four steps plus a check (make test) that proves it worked.
Index the skill
Store the skill under its description, with the commit it was learned on and a failure counter, so it can be found and audited later.
Retrieve at the start of a task
A new task, adding a /payouts endpoint, matches the skill with similarity 0.86, above the 0.80 threshold, so the agent loads the skill instead of exploring.
Follow it and verify
The agent finishes in 4 steps instead of 9 and runs the skill’s check. Verification is what makes reuse safe.
Revise or retire
After a refactor the skill fails its check twice, so it is retired and the next run explores and learns a fresh version.

steps: Store episodes, extract a graph
Each note or conversation is added as an episode. The library extracts entities (Priya, account 4471, Rahul, Sunita) and the relationships between them.
Record when each fact became true
The reference time says when the note applies. Every edge gets a valid-from time, and the system also records when it learned the fact.
Close contradicted facts
The new nominee contradicts “Rahul is nominee”, so that edge gets an end date. Nothing is deleted, so you can still say who was nominee in 2024.
Search the graph for the current state
A question is answered by searching edges and text together, preferring facts that are valid now.
Show when the answer was true
The answer carries its validity: Sunita, nominee since 10 June 2025. A relationship manager can see the history.
Test multi-hop questions
Measure on questions that chain facts, such as “the nominee on the account opened after the address change”. Here accuracy rises from 45% to 85%.

lib: messages.count_tokens returns the input token count for a request before you send it, so you can budget each segment.
code:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-5"          # use your current model
BUDGET = 8_000                       # effective budget found by your own length eval

def tokens(text: str) -> int:
    r = client.messages.count_tokens(model=MODEL,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}])
    return r.input_tokens

def build_prompt(question: str, clauses: list[tuple[float, str]]) -> str:
    kept, used = [], tokens(question)
    for score, text in sorted(clauses, reverse=True):     # highest relevance first
        t = tokens(text)
        if used + t > BUDGET:
            break
        kept.append(text); used += t
    docs = "\n".join(f"<clause>{c}</clause>" for c in kept)
    return f"{docs}\n\nQuestion: {question}"               # documents first, query last
ctxbudget.note: score each clause with your retriever or re-ranker; count_tokens is a free endpoint with its own rate limits, so cache counts for fixed clauses.

from mem0 import Memory

m = Memory()                          # default config; set your LLM and vector store

def remember(user_id: str, user_msg: str, reply: str):
    m.add([{"role": "user", "content": user_msg},
           {"role": "assistant", "content": reply}],
          user_id=user_id)            # extract + reconcile, scoped to this investor

def recall(user_id: str, question: str, k: int = 3) -> str:
    hits = m.search(question, user_id=user_id, limit=k)["results"]
    return "\n".join(f"- {h['memory']}" for h in hits)

facts = recall("inv-2231", "Which city is the investor in?")
system = f"Known facts about this investor:\n{facts}"   # near the top of the prompt

code:
from pathlib import Path
import anthropic

ROOT = Path("./memories").resolve()
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def safe(p: str) -> Path:
    full = (ROOT / p.removeprefix("/memories").lstrip("/")).resolve()
    if not full.is_relative_to(ROOT):                  # resolve first, then check
        raise ValueError("path outside /memories")
    return full

def handle(cmd: dict) -> str:
    if cmd["command"] == "view":
        p = safe(cmd["path"])
        return "\n".join(x.name for x in p.iterdir()) if p.is_dir() else p.read_text()
    if cmd["command"] == "create":
        p = safe(cmd["path"]); p.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        p.write_text(cmd["file_text"]); return "saved"
    ...                                                # str_replace, insert, delete, rename

r = client.beta.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-5", max_tokens=2048,        # use your current model
    betas=["context-management-2025-06-27"],
    tools=[{"type": "memory_20250818", "name": "memory"}],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Continue the ITR checklist for client 114."}])

import asyncio
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from graphiti_core import Graphiti
from graphiti_core.nodes import EpisodeType

async def main():
    graph = Graphiti("bolt://localhost:7687", "neo4j", "password")
    await graph.build_indices_and_constraints()
    for when, text in [
        (datetime(2024, 3, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc), "Priya made Rahul nominee on account 4471."),
        (datetime(2025, 6, 10, tzinfo=timezone.utc), "Priya changed the nominee on account 4471 to Sunita."),
    ]:
        await graph.add_episode(name=f"note-{when.date()}", episode_body=text,
                                source=EpisodeType.text, source_description="RM note",
                                reference_time=when)
    for edge in await graph.search("Who is the nominee on account 4471?"):
        print(edge.fact, edge.valid_at, edge.invalid_at)
    await graph.close()

asyncio.run(main())

ctxbudget.title: Prompt builder “for balance”
ctxbudget.code:
def build_prompt(question, chunks, k=7):
    top = sorted(chunks, key=lambda c: c.score, reverse=True)[:k]
    mid = len(top) // 2
    ordered = top[1:mid + 1] + [top[0]] + top[mid + 1:]   # best chunk in the centre
    docs = "\n\n".join(c.text for c in ordered)
    return f"{docs}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
ctxbudget.explain: Moving the top chunk to the centre places the most relevant text exactly where long-context models use information worst (lost in the middle). Keep the ranked order so the best chunk is first, with the question last.

also.2: Sorting by score, highest first, is correct.
also.6: Putting the question after the documents is correct: long documents first, query last.

stm.title: Trim history to fit the budget
stm.explain: pop(0) removes the first message, which holds the task and constraints, so the agent keeps talking but forgets what it is doing. Pin the first message and drop or summarize the oldest turns after it.
stm.fix: messages.pop(1)                    # keep messages[0]; drop the oldest turn after it

also.3: Looping until the count fits the budget is fine; the problem is which message is dropped.

semmem.title: Recall facts for this investor
semmem.explain: The namespace ("memories",) is shared by everyone, so the search can return another investor’s facts. Put the tenant and user ID in the namespace for every search and write.

also.3: Reading h.value["text"] is fine if facts were stored under that key.

epimem.title: Score past episodes
epimem.code:
def score(ep, now_h, query_vec):
    recency = 0.995 ** (now_h - ep.hour)        # 0 to 1
    importance = ep.importance                  # 1 to 10
    relevance = cosine(query_vec, ep.vec)       # 0 to 1
    return recency + importance + relevance
epimem.explain: The three scores are on different scales, so importance (1 to 10) swamps recency and relevance (0 to 1): any important episode wins, however unrelated. Min-max normalize each score across candidates, then weight and add.
epimem.fix: return w_r * norm_rec[ep.id] + w_i * norm_imp[ep.id] + w_s * norm_rel[ep.id]   # each min-max normalized

also.2: 0.995 per hour is the decay factor used in Generative Agents.
also.4: Cosine similarity for relevance is standard.

memwrite.title: Honour an erasure request
memwrite.code:
def delete_user(uid):
    n = db.execute("DELETE FROM memories WHERE user_id = %s", (uid,))
    audit.log("erasure", user=uid, rows=n)
    return n
memwrite.explain: Only the table rows are deleted. The embeddings in the vector index, rolling summaries and caches still hold the data, so it can be retrieved again. Delete every copy, then log.
memwrite.fix:
n = db.execute("DELETE FROM memories WHERE user_id = %s", (uid,))
    vectors.delete(filter={"user_id": uid}); summaries.delete(uid); cache.delete(uid)

also.3: Logging the erasure without the data is exactly what an audit trail needs.

memtools.title: Validate memory paths
memtools.explain: A prefix check on the raw string lets /memories/../secrets.txt through: it starts with /memories but resolves outside it. Resolve the path first, then check that it is inside the root.

also.7: Raising PermissionError on a refused path is the right behaviour.

procmem.title: Reusing and saving procedures
procmem.explain: Every run is saved, including ones whose tests failed, so the agent memorizes broken procedures and replays them with confidence. Record a trajectory only after it has been verified.
procmem.fix:
if result.tests_passed:               # verified runs only
        store.record(task, result.steps)

also.3: Reusing only at or above the threshold is correct; the threshold value itself is a tuning choice.
also.6: Exploring when nothing matches is the right fallback.

graphmem.title: Updating a nominee
graphmem.code:
def change_nominee(graph, account, new_nominee, when):
    old = graph.find_edge(account, "nominee_of")
    graph.delete_edge(old)
    graph.add_edge(new_nominee, "nominee_of", account, valid_from=when)
graphmem.explain: Deleting the old edge loses the history: nobody can later say who was nominee when a claim was filed in 2024. Close the old edge with an end date instead.

also.2: Finding the current edge first is right.
also.4: Adding the new edge with a valid-from date is right.

2: The model advertises a 200k window. What budget do we set?
The length where our own eval stays accurate
200k, so nothing is ever cut
Advertised length is not effective length. The budget comes from measuring accuracy at different lengths on your task.
3: The budget is 16k. Which chunks go in?
A random sample so the prompt stays varied
The highest-scoring chunks until the budget is spent
Rank by relevance and fill the budget from the top; low-signal chunks become distractors.
4: Where should the question go?
After the documents, at the end
Before the documents, so the model knows what to look for
Anthropic’s guidance is long documents first, query last, which scored up to 30% better in its tests.
5: The other 55 clauses might be needed later. What do we give the agent?
Their full text, just in case
A short index of IDs and a tool to fetch one
Just-in-time loading keeps the window small and lets the agent pull a clause only when needed.
6: What should re-testing at 128k show?
The same accuracy as at 8k
A drop, which is why the budget exists
Accuracy falls with length even on simple tasks. The drop is the evidence for the budget.

2: Context grows 4.5k a turn from 4k. When does it pass 150k?
Around turn 33
Around turn 90
3: Which is the safest thing to remove first?
Old tool results, which can be fetched again
The oldest conversation turns
Tool-result clearing is one of the safest reductions: the call stays recorded and the data can be re-fetched.
4: What must the compaction instructions say?
Keep it short: one paragraph at most
Copy IDs, amounts, decisions and open tasks verbatim
Summaries tend to paraphrase. Naming the values to copy exactly is what keeps them intact.
5: After a compaction, how does the agent know what is left to do?
It re-reads a progress note
It infers it from the summary alone
A short note of decisions and open tasks is re-read after each compaction, so work resumes in the right place.
6: How do you know compaction kept what mattered?
Probe with questions about early turns
Check that the summary is shorter than the history
Only a probe shows whether the loan account and EMI survived. Length says nothing about accuracy.

2: What does the extraction step produce?
Short candidate facts
A summary of the whole session
Extraction turns each exchange into small facts that can be compared and updated one by one.
3: The investor says “We moved to Bengaluru”. What happens to “lives in Pune”?
It is updated to Bengaluru
A second city fact is added
Reconciliation compares the new fact with similar stored ones and chooses UPDATE, so there is one current city.
4: Where does the investor ID go?
Only in the prompt text
In the namespace of every write and search
Scoping in the storage layer prevents one investor’s facts from being retrieved for another.
5: How much memory goes into the prompt each turn?
Every stored fact about the investor
The few facts most relevant to the question
Top-k retrieval injects about 180 tokens instead of 26k of transcripts.
6: The investor never mentioned an employer. What is the right answer?
“I don’t know”
The most likely employer from similar investors
Abstention is part of memory quality: an invented fact is worse than admitting none is stored.

2: Which episode gets the higher importance score?
“Customer said thanks”
A PAN lookup that timed out and kept a customer waiting
Importance is rated when the episode is written; failures with customer impact score high.
3: Why normalize the three scores before adding them?
Importance runs 1–10 and would swamp the 0–1 scores
Normalizing makes retrieval faster
Without normalization the component with the largest range decides every ranking.
4: When does the agent reflect?
After every single episode
When recent importance adds up past a threshold such as 150
Generative Agents reflect when summed importance of recent events passes 150, about two or three times a day.
5: What goes into the prompt for the new PAN task?
Five full transcripts of similar runs
A 40-token lesson citing those runs
Lessons are shorter and generalize better than transcripts.
6: Which number shows episodic memory is working?
How many episodes are stored
How often the agent repeats a known mistake
Storage size says nothing; a falling repeat-error rate is the outcome you want.

2: The customer asked for today’s gold rate. Save it?
No: it is a one-off, not a reusable fact
Yes: everything the customer says may matter later
Only stable, reusable facts earn a place; one-off remarks become noise.
3: A new address arrives. What happens to the old one?
It is deleted with no trace
It is invalidated with a date and kept as history
Invalidating keeps history for audit while retrieval sees only the current fact.
4: What happens to the “app crashed” complaint?
It expires after 30 days
It is kept forever in case it recurs
A TTL lets one-off items expire so the store does not fill with stale noise.
5: The customer requests erasure. Which copies must go?
The table rows
Rows, vectors, summaries and caches
Every derived copy can bring the data back; deletion must reach them all.
6: What does the weekly audit look for?
Blocked patterns, expired items still present, deletions with no audit line
How many memories were added
Audits check that the policy is actually being enforced, not just how much was written.

2: Where are the memory files actually stored?
In your own storage, through the handlers you write
On Anthropic’s servers
The memory tool is client-side: Claude sends commands and your code carries them out.
3: Is /memories/../config.env allowed?
No: it resolves outside the memory root
Yes: it starts with /memories
Resolve first, then check. The ../ segment takes it outside the root.
4: The agent starts a new session. What does it do first?
Starts the checklist from item 1
Views its memory and resumes from progress.md
Viewing memory first is what lets it resume at item 13 instead of redoing work.
5: Why pair the memory tool with context editing?
The agent can save what matters before old tool results are cleared
Context editing replaces the memory tool
Clearing keeps sessions small; memory keeps what the cleared results taught.
6: Why log every memory write?
So people can review what the agent chose to remember
Logs make writes faster
Agent-managed memory is less predictable, so writes need review.

2: Three verified runs of the same kind exist. What becomes the skill?
One procedure distilled from them, with a check at the end
All three trajectories, stored as they are
A skill is one reusable procedure, ideally the shortest that worked, ending with a check that proves success.
3: How should the skill be stored so it can be found and audited later?
Inside the system prompt of every run
Indexed by its description, with the commit it was learned on
Retrieval by description finds it when relevant; the commit and failure count show when it may be stale.
4: A new task matches with similarity 0.86 and the threshold is 0.80. What does the agent do?
Loads the skill and follows it
Explores from scratch to be safe
At or above the threshold, the agent reuses the stored procedure.
5: The agent follows the 4-step skill. Is it finished?
Only after the skill’s check passes
Yes: the steps worked before
Verification is what makes reuse safe. The codebase may have changed since the skill was saved.
6: After a refactor, the skill fails its check twice. What should happen?
Keep it: it worked many times
Retire or revise it and let the next run re-learn
Stale procedures replay outdated steps confidently. Failures are the signal to retire them.

2: Why record a reference time for each note?
So each fact knows when it became true
To sort notes alphabetically
Valid time is what lets the agent answer “as of” questions.
3: The nominee changes. What happens to the old edge?
It gets an end date
It is deleted
Closing keeps history and still answers the present correctly.
4: Which facts should answer “who is the nominee now”?
Edges valid now
All edges ever recorded
Filter to currently valid edges.
5: Why show when the answer became true?
So people can see and check the history
It is required by Neo4j
Dated answers are easier to trust and audit.
6: Which questions show the biggest gain over vector memory?
Multi-hop questions that chain facts
Single-fact lookups
Traversing relationships is what graphs add.
