A 120-turn session sends 19.8M input tokens unmanaged and 6.4M with clearing and compaction. About what percentage is saved?
A tutoring agent keeps a “progress note” file. When should it re-read it?
Only at the start of the course
Re-reading the note after compaction restores decisions and open tasks the summary may compress.
Anthropic lists techniques for long-horizon tasks. Which are among them? Select all that apply.
Compaction, notes and sub-agents are the named techniques; temperature does not manage context.
Which tool should be listed in exclude_tools when clearing results in a loan call?
A search tool whose old results are no longer used
get_loan_summary, which the agent keeps referring to
Exclude tools whose results are still referenced; clear the rest.
Anthropic reported that context editing cut token use in a 100-turn web-search evaluation by about how much?
Anthropic reported an 84% reduction in token consumption for that evaluation.
A rebooking chat is compacted 7 times in one session and fare details start to drift. What is the best structural fix?
Clear bulky tool results first so compaction runs less often
Clearing the bulk reduces how often history must be summarized, and each summary-of-a-summary risks drift.
Which checks show that a compaction policy is safe to ship? Select all that apply.
Comparing answers with an uncompacted baseline
Checking only that the summary is shorter
Counting how many summaries were written
Probes and baseline comparison test what survived; length and counts do not.
A session’s context grows 1k of talk plus a 3k tool result per turn. Clearing keeps only the last 2 results. After 50 turns, with no compaction and a 4k pinned start, what is the context?
semmem: An investor said “I live in Pune” in January and “we moved to Bengaluru” in June. An append-only store now holds both. What is the risk?
The assistant may retrieve the old city and act on it
The store will refuse the second fact
Append-only memory keeps contradictions; retrieval can surface the stale fact.
Mem0 compares each candidate fact with similar stored memories and chooses one of which operations?
ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or no change
Mem0’s reconciliation step picks ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP.
Which make a semantic memory store safe for a multi-tenant telecom assistant? Select all that apply.
Tenant and user ID in the namespace of every write and search
Enforcing scope in the storage layer
One shared namespace for faster search
Telling the model in the prompt not to mention other users
Scoping must be structural. A shared namespace leaks; prompt instructions are not a control.
Replaying full history costs 26,000 tokens per turn; retrieving 3 facts costs 180. What percentage is saved?
A tutor asks “When is the learner’s exam?” The learner never said. What should memory-backed answers do?
Ask the model to invent a plausible one
Abstention is part of memory quality; LongMemEval tests it explicitly.
A LangGraph store search uses the namespace ("memories",) for all customers. What is the bug?
All customers share one namespace, so facts can leak between them
Namespaces must be strings, not tuples
The namespace must include the user (and tenant) ID.
Which facts are good candidates for semantic memory in a shopping assistant? Select all that apply.
The exact wording of a greeting last week
Stable, reusable facts belong in semantic memory; greetings and short-lived prices do not.
Graphiti handles a contradicted fact (old nominee replaced by a new one) how?
Deletes the old fact with no trace
Invalidates it with a validity window and keeps history
Graphiti keeps temporal validity, so history questions still work while retrieval uses the current fact.
Each fact costs about 60 tokens. A profile document has a 40-token header and 5 facts. How many tokens does injecting it cost?
A clinic assistant should remember appointment preferences across months. Which technique is this?
Durable facts about a user across sessions are semantic memory.
LongMemEval evaluates which abilities? Select all that apply.
It tests extraction, multi-session and temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention.
A customer’s plan changed from Basic to Premium. The store still returns Basic first. With append-only memory, which quick mitigation helps answers but leaves the store stale?
Newest-wins fixes the answer when both are retrieved, but the stale fact is still stored; reconciliation is the real fix.
On LOCOMO, Mem0 reported token savings versus full-context replay of roughly what size?
Mem0 reported over 90% token savings compared with full context.
Which statements about profile versus collection memory are correct? Select all that apply.
A profile is one document per user, rewritten as facts change
A collection stores many small facts and retrieves a few
A profile must be retrieved with top-k
A collection can never be updated
Profiles are single documents; collections are many small items retrieved by relevance. Both can be updated.
An assistant keeps 8 facts, 3 of them stale. After switching to reconciliation, how many facts remain if each stale fact was replaced by a newer one already stored?
The 3 stale facts are removed and their replacements stay: 8 − 3 = 5.
Where should retrieved investor facts go in the prompt?
Near the top, in a clearly marked block
Buried in the middle of the conversation history
Only in the assistant’s previous reply
In a tool result with no label
A clearly labelled block near the top is easy for the model to find and use.
Top-k is 1 and the SIP fact ranks second for “What is the monthly SIP?”. What happens?
The assistant has no SIP fact and should say it does not know
Only the top-ranked fact is retrieved, and it is not the SIP fact.
Which are risks of semantic memory in a patient-facing assistant? Select all that apply.
Facts leaking across patients without scoping
Staleness and leakage are the risks; lower tokens and faster retrieval are benefits.
A dispatcher assistant stores “preferred depot: Bhiwandi” and later “switched to Taloja”. With reconciliation, what does the store hold?
Only Taloja as the current depot
The new statement updates the existing depot fact.
Which tool is built around a temporal knowledge graph for agent memory?
Graphiti, from Zep, builds a temporal knowledge graph with validity windows.
epimem: Recency decays by 0.995 per hour. What is the recency of an episode 100 hours old, to two decimals?
An episode score adds raw recency (0–1), importance (1–10) and relevance (0–1). What goes wrong?
Importance swamps the other two, so any important episode wins
Different scales must be normalized before weighting.
Which scores does the Generative Agents retrieval function combine? Select all that apply.
Recency, importance and relevance, each normalized, are combined.
An incident agent keeps retrieving “user said thanks” from an hour ago instead of a similar outage from last month. Which weight is too high?
A recency weight that is too high lets trivial recent events win.
In Generative Agents, reflection fires when the summed importance of recent events passes what threshold?
The paper uses a threshold of 150, which produced about 2–3 reflections a day.
Reflexion reported what pass@1 on HumanEval, compared with 80% for GPT-4?
Reflexion reported 91% pass@1 versus 80% for GPT-4.
Which belong in an episode record for a payment-failure agent? Select all that apply.
Task, steps, outcome, time and cost describe an episode; card numbers must never be stored.
Min-max normalizing importance scores of 2, 5 and 8 gives what for the score 5?
Five transcripts cost 350 tokens each; one reflected lesson costs 40 tokens. How many tokens does the lesson save?
What is the best success metric for an incident agent’s episodic memory?
Whether the agent stops repeating known mistakes is what matters.
A reflection says “Customs API fails on Fridays; switch to manual filing.” Which safeguards are sensible? Select all that apply.
Cite the episodes the lesson came from
Review or retire the lesson when new evidence contradicts it
Inject it into every prompt forever, regardless of task
Cited, reviewable lessons can be checked; permanent injection and deleting evidence make errors stick.
Episode A is 504 hours old; episode B is 1 hour old. What is A’s recency at 0.995 per hour, to two decimals?
With equal weights on normalized scores, an old failure has recency 0, importance 1 and relevance 1. A trivial recent chat has 1, 0 and 0. Which ranks higher?
How does LangGraph describe episodic memory in agents?
Past experiences, often used as few-shot examples
LangGraph frames episodic memory as past experiences, often used as examples.
A triage agent’s episodic memory keeps ranking unrelated high-importance episodes first. Which changes help? Select all that apply.
Rebalancing toward relevance fixes it; dropping normalization or relevance makes it worse.
When is episodic memory the wrong fix?
The agent repeats last week’s deployment mistake
Failures are about a user’s outdated profile facts
Past incidents predict the right fix
Stale user facts are a semantic-memory problem.
Top-k is 3 and the relevant failure ranks 10 of 12. After rebalancing it ranks 1. How many prompt tokens does top-k 3 cost at 350 per transcript?
Importance is rated when an episode is written. Who usually rates it?
An LLM prompt returning a score from 1 to 10
Generative Agents ask the model to rate importance on a 1–10 scale.
Which statements about reflection are correct? Select all that apply.
It condenses episodes into higher-level lessons
It removes the need to log episodes
Reflection condenses and saves tokens, but lessons can be wrong and still need their source episodes.
Scores normalized: recency 0.2, importance 0.9, relevance 0.8. Weights 1, 1, 2. What is the total?
memwrite: A customer asks the bank assistant to erase their data. Engineering deletes the memory rows. What is still wrong?
Vectors, summaries and caches may still hold the data
The audit log must also be deleted
Erasure must reach every derived copy; a minimal audit line without the data is kept as proof.
Which should never be written to an assistant’s long-term memory? Select all that apply.
OTPs and card numbers must be blocked; language and channel preferences are useful, safe facts.
A policyholder’s old and new addresses are both stored as valid. What policy fixes this?
Keep both; the model will choose
Newer wins; the older is invalidated with a date
Consolidating conflicts keeps one current fact and history for audit.
A user’s data sits in 4 rows, 4 vectors, 1 summary and 1 cache entry. Deletion removes only the rows. What percentage of copies survive?
Under India’s DPDP Act, section 8(7), when must a data fiduciary erase personal data?
Never, if it might be useful
When consent is withdrawn or the purpose is no longer served, unless law requires retention
Only when a court orders it
Section 8(7) requires erasure on withdrawal of consent or when the purpose ends, subject to legal retention. This is a summary, not legal advice.
“App crashed on login” is saved as a memory. What should happen to it?
Give it a TTL so it expires, for example after 30 days
Promote it to the system prompt
One-off items should expire so the store does not fill with stale noise.
Which are sound parts of a memory write policy? Select all that apply.
Pattern and PII filters before writing
Saving everything and filtering at read time
Keeping contradictory facts with no dates
Allow-lists and pre-write filters work; read-time filtering still stores the data, and undated contradictions cause stale answers.
DPDP Rules 2025 require processing logs to be kept for at least how long?
Rule 8 requires the logs to be kept for at least one year. This is a summary, not legal advice.
LangGraph describes two times to write memory. Which is the trade-off of writing in the hot path?
It is immediate but adds latency to the response
Hot-path writes are available immediately but add latency; background writes are cheaper but delayed.
Ten candidates arrive; 3 are sensitive, 2 are one-offs and 1 is an outdated address. With filters, a stability threshold and conflict handling, how many valid memories remain?
A patient requests erasure. Which must the system delete? Select all that apply.
The audit line recording that the erasure happened
Rows, embeddings and summaries are copies. The audit line, without the data, is proof of deletion.
A stability threshold of 0.8 blocks an OTP scored 0.6 but lets a PAN scored 0.88 through. What is the lesson?
Stability is not sensitivity; add a sensitive-data filter
Sensitive items can look stable; they need a separate filter.
What do Letta sleep-time agents do?
Consolidate and rewrite memory in the background
Delete all memories after a session
Sleep-time agents modify memory asynchronously, between conversations.
A regex blocks 12-digit numbers to stop Aadhaar numbers being stored. What does it miss?
Numbers written with spaces or in words, and other identifiers
Pattern filters are a first line; add a PII detector such as Presidio and allow-lists.
An erasure removes rows and vectors but not the rolling summary or cache. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
The data can still reach the model through the summary
The cache may serve the old profile
Only an audit line should remain after erasure
Leftover summaries and caches keep the data retrievable; only an audit line should remain.
A bank must keep KYC records by law but has received an erasure request for the assistant’s memory. What is the right design?
Keep KYC records in the system of record; erase the assistant’s memory copies
Move the KYC records into assistant memory
Legal retention applies to the system of record; agent memory should not hold those records.
Stored memories: 9 items with a row and a vector each, plus 1 summary and 1 cache. How many copies exist?
What should a weekly memory audit check?
Blocked patterns present, expired items still stored, deletions without audit lines
Audits verify that the policy is enforced.
Which are valid forgetting mechanisms? Select all that apply.
TTLs, decay and deletion are forgetting mechanisms; duplication makes forgetting harder.
Under DPDP Rule 8, how much notice must be given before erasure after the Third Schedule period ends?
Rule 8 requires 48 hours’ notice before erasure. This is a summary, not legal advice.
memtools: A memory handler checks path.startswith("/memories"). Which path wrongly passes?
It starts with /memories but resolves outside; resolve first, then check the root.
Which commands does Claude’s memory tool (memory_20250818) support? Select all that apply.
It supports view, create, str_replace, insert, delete and rename; there is no execute.
Where are the memory tool’s files stored?
Client-side, in storage your handlers manage
The memory tool is client-side: you implement the handlers and storage.
Three sessions cost 160k each without memory. With memory they cost 90k, 60k and 60k. What percentage is saved?
Which paper framed agent-managed memory as an operating system paging between a small main context and larger stores?
MemGPT introduced virtual context management with memory tiers.
Which make memory tool handlers safer? Select all that apply.
Resolve the path, then check it is inside the root
Resolved-path checks and tenant isolation help; unrestricted symlinks and no logs are unsafe.
An agent writes progress every 5 items. A session ends after item 12. Where does the next session resume?
The last saved checkpoint is item 10, so it resumes at item 11 and redoes 11 and 12.
In Anthropic’s evaluation, memory tool plus context editing improved performance by about how much over baseline?
Anthropic reported a 39% improvement with both; 84% was the token reduction from context editing.
When is agent-managed memory a poor fit?
Regulated customer data where every write must follow a fixed schema
Predictable, auditable writes favour a developer-run pipeline.
A session fits 16 items. The agent writes progress every item. How many sessions does a 30-item checklist need?
Letta memory blocks have which properties? Select all that apply.
A description that guides the agent
Blocks have a label, value, limit and description; there is no GPU field.
Which Letta tools let an agent write to and search archival memory?
Letta’s archival memory uses archival_memory_insert and archival_memory_search.
Python: (ROOT / "../config.env").resolve() lands outside ROOT. Which check catches it?
Resolve first, then test containment with is_relative_to.
Why pair the memory tool with context editing?
The agent can save key information before old tool results are cleared
Claude is warned near the clearing threshold and can save what matters to memory first.
A clinic agent can write its own memory. Which risks need controls? Select all that apply.
Writing patient health details into notes
Storing instructions that change its future behaviour
Reading its progress file at session start
Sensitive data and injected instructions need filters and review; reading progress and resuming are the intended use.
Each item costs 7k tokens, start-up 4k and each progress write 1k. A session does 16 items and writes 3 times. What does it cost?
What should the agent do first in a new session with the memory tool?
Viewing memory first is what lets it resume progress.
A path /memories/clients/../progress.md is requested. After resolving, where does it point?
clients/.. cancels out, leaving /memories/progress.md, which is inside the root.
Which belong in a review process for agent-written memory? Select all that apply.
Logging every write with its path
Letting the agent approve its own writes
Logs and sampling support review; self-approval and deleting logs defeat it.
Progress is written every 10 items; sessions fit 16. Starting at item 1, how many items are redone across sessions 1 and 2?
Session 1 does 1–16 and saves 10; session 2 restarts at 11, redoing 11–16: 6 items.
procmem: Every Monday a coding agent spends 20 minutes rediscovering how the team deploys a hotfix: which branch, which checks, which approvals. What is the most direct fix?
Switch to a model with a larger context window
Save the verified deployment routine as a skill the agent retrieves when the task matches
Add more tools to the agent
The routine is stable and repeated, which is exactly what procedural memory is for: solve once, reuse many times.
You are writing a skill for “add an API endpoint to the payments service”. What belongs in it? Select all that apply.
The files to touch and the patterns to copy
A final check, such as make test, that proves it worked
A specific description of when the skill applies
The full transcripts of every past run
A skill is a concise, reusable procedure with a check and a description for retrieval. Raw transcripts are episodic records and waste context.
Without a skill a catalogue-import task takes 11 steps; with it, 5. It runs 30 times a month at about 2,500 tokens per step. How many tokens does the skill save per month?
(11 − 5) steps × 2,500 tokens × 30 runs = 450,000 tokens a month.
After a database schema migration, the claims team’s coding agent keeps producing migrations that fail review, always using the same saved procedure. What is the most likely cause?
The model has become less capable
The saved procedure is stale and still encodes the old schema
The retrieval threshold is too high
Prefix caching is serving old outputs
Stale procedures replay outdated steps with confidence. Track failures per skill and revise or retire it.
At a retrieval threshold of 0.60, the agent loads the “add endpoint” skill for a task about rotating API keys, then wastes steps backtracking. What should you change first?
Raise the threshold and sharpen the skill’s description, then measure on real tasks
Add the rotation steps to the endpoint skill
A loose threshold causes wrong retrievals. Tune it on labelled tasks and make descriptions specific about when the skill applies.
Which details should be stored with each saved skill so it can be audited later? Select all that apply.
The commit or date it was learned on
How many times its check has failed
Patient records that appeared in the run it came from
Provenance and failure counts show when a skill may be stale. Never store sensitive data such as patient records in memory.
A support agent “knows” that the billing service is written in Go and owned by the payments team. Which kind of memory is this?
Facts about the world or codebase are semantic memory. Procedural memory is how to do something.
An agent recalls that on 3 March it failed to reconcile an exchange trade file because of a time-zone bug. Which kind of memory is this?
A record of a specific past event is episodic memory. Distilled into a rule or routine, it could become procedural.
In the Voyager research agent, what does the skill library contain?
Executable programs, retrieved by matching their descriptions to the current task
Voyager stores working code as skills, indexed by description, and composes them for new tasks.
A Claude Code skill lives in a folder with a SKILL.md file. What mainly decides whether the agent loads it for a task?
The skill’s description matching the task, or the user invoking it by name
The description is what the agent matches against; a skill’s body loads only when it is used.
Exploring takes 9 steps, following the right skill 4, following a wrong skill 12. Of 10 tasks, 6 reuse correctly, 2 load the wrong skill and 2 are explored. What is the average steps per task?
Which are signs that a saved procedure should be revised or retired? Select all that apply.
Its check has failed on the last few reuses
An API it calls has been deprecated
It has been reused 200 times successfully
The part of the codebase it touches was refactored
Failures, deprecations and refactors signal staleness. Many successful reuses are a reason to keep it.
A team proposes saving every agent trajectory as memory “so nothing is lost”. What is the better policy?
Save everything; retrieval will sort it out
Save only repeated routines from verified, successful runs, after review
Save only failed runs, to learn from them
Save nothing and rely on the model
Saving everything memorizes mistakes and floods retrieval. Keep verified, reviewed procedures.
When is a repository instruction file such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md enough, without separate skills?
For short conventions that apply to almost every task, such as “run make lint before committing”
Always-on files suit short, universal rules. Long procedures belong in skills that load only when relevant.
A skill cuts a task from 8 steps to 3, and it applies to 40% of tasks; the rest still take 8. What is the new average steps per task?
What can go wrong with procedural memory that nobody reviews? Select all that apply.
It can store unsafe shortcuts, such as skipping tests
It can replay a mistake on every future run
It can capture secrets that appeared during a run
It makes the model’s weights larger
Memory is data the agent trusts. Review it like code. It does not change model weights.
What does the Agent Workflow Memory approach do?
Induces reusable workflows from past trajectories and gives them to the agent on new tasks
Fine-tunes the model on every run
It extracts common sub-routines from past runs and supplies them as guidance, improving success on web-navigation tasks.
Skill descriptions such as “helper for backend stuff” cause poor retrieval. What fixes it?
Specific descriptions of what the skill does and when to use it
Retrieval matches the task against the description, so it must say precisely what the skill is for.
A successful run that added a UPI payment method took 14 steps, including a 5-step dead end. What should the saved skill contain?
All 14 steps, exactly as they happened
The cleaned-up 9 steps that mattered, plus a check
Only the dead end, as a warning
Nothing; one run is not enough to save
Distil the working path without detours and end with a check. The dead end can be a one-line warning.
Which metrics show whether a skill library is actually helping? Select all that apply.
Outcomes and costs matter. The number of stored skills is a vanity metric.
graphmem: What does a temporal knowledge graph add to plain facts?
Relationships between entities with the time each was true
A policyholder changes address. What should memory do?
Close the old address with an end date and add the new one
Closing keeps history and a correct present.
Who is nominee on the account Priya opened after her address change?
It chains an address change, an account and a nominee.
Which belong on a temporal edge? Select all that apply.
Valid time versus recorded time: which is when the fact was true in the world?
Recorded time is when the system learned it.
Why can vector memory return stale facts?
Old and new sentences are both similar to the question and carry no validity
70% simple at 95% and 30% multi-hop at 85%. Overall?
What is a main cost of graph memory?
LLM calls to extract entities and relationships
An auditor asks who was nominee on 1 January 2025. What makes this answerable?
Keeping closed edges with their dates
Which are risks of automatic extraction? Select all that apply.
Stale facts fall from 16 to 1 per 100 queries. Out of 5,000 queries, how many fewer stale facts?
Which library builds temporal knowledge graphs for agent memory?
A consent was withdrawn. What should the graph do?
End the consent edge at the withdrawal date
When memory is a few stable preferences
Simple stores suffice for simple memory.
How should a question “who is the account holder now?” be answered?
Which help answer questions from graph memory? Select all that apply.
Text or vector search for fuzzy names
A customer asks to be forgotten under the DPDP Act. What happens in graph memory?
Delete the person’s entities, edges and source episodes
Erasure differs from closing a changed fact.
Extraction costs 1,500 tokens per fact at ₹0.25 per 1,000. What do 1,000 facts cost?
Two notes disagree about a nominee on the same date. What should the system do?
Which store handles “what did we know on 1 March?” best?
Recorded time answers what was known when.

ctxbudget.q: Your team wants a 1M-token model so the agent can “see everything”. How do you respond?
pts: effective length is shorter than advertised
ctxbudget.model: A bigger window does not mean better use of it. Accuracy falls as input grows even on simple tasks, facts in the middle are used worst, and benchmarks such as RULER show that effective length is often far below the advertised maximum. Measure accuracy at your real lengths, set a budget, and fill it with the highest-signal chunks, with the question last.

ctxbudget.q: How would you find the right context budget for a contract-review agent?
pts: an eval set of real questions
ctxbudget.model: Build an eval set of real contract questions with known answers, run it with inputs padded to several lengths such as 8k, 32k and 128k, and set the budget below the length where accuracy starts to fall. Re-run it whenever the model or the retriever changes.

ctxbudget.q: Why load context “just in time” instead of up front?
pts: IDs or an index instead of full text
ctxbudget.model: Up-front loading fills the window with text the agent may never need, adding cost and distractors. Passing lightweight references such as IDs and titles, plus a tool to fetch full content, keeps the window small and lets the agent load only what the current step needs.

stm.q: Explain the difference between tool-result clearing and compaction, and when you use each.
stm.model: Clearing replaces old tool results with placeholders while the call stays recorded; the data can be fetched again, so it is one of the safest reductions and comes first. Compaction summarizes the conversation itself when clearing is not enough, so it needs instructions that keep identifiers, amounts, decisions and open tasks verbatim.

stm.q: How do clearing and compaction interact with prompt caching?
stm.model: Both rewrite earlier content, so the cached prefix no longer matches from that point and the next request pays full price for it. Clearing a large amount at a time, with a setting such as clear_at_least, means fewer rewrites for the same saving.

stm.q: How would you prove that compaction is safe for a two-hour loan call?
stm.model: Replay long recorded calls, compact them, and probe the agent with questions about early turns whose answers are exact: the loan account, agreed EMI and mandate status. Compare with an uncompacted baseline, and if a value is paraphrased or lost, tighten the compaction instructions before shipping.

semmem.q: Why is an append-only memory store dangerous for a wealth assistant?
semmem.model: Appending keeps both the old and the new fact, so retrieval may surface the outdated risk profile or address, and the assistant advises on it confidently. Reconcile each new fact with similar stored ones and update or invalidate the old one.

semmem.q: Design memory scoping for a multi-tenant advisory product.
pts: tenant and user in the namespace
enforced in storage, not the prompt
semmem.model: Put the tenant and user ID in the namespace of every write and search, enforce it in the storage layer rather than trusting the prompt, and add tests that try to retrieve one user’s facts while acting as another.

semmem.q: How do you evaluate semantic memory beyond recall?
semmem.model: Benchmarks such as LongMemEval test extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention. Include questions whose answer changed, questions about when something was true, and questions the user never answered, where the right answer is “I don’t know”.

epimem.q: Explain how an agent should choose which past episodes to recall.
epimem.model: Score each episode on recency (exponential decay with age), importance (rated when written) and relevance (similarity to the current situation). Min-max normalize each score so no scale dominates, weight and add them, and retrieve the top few.

epimem.q: What does reflection add, and what are its risks?
epimem.model: Reflection turns several related episodes into a short lesson the agent can inject cheaply, which generalizes better than transcripts. Lessons can be wrong or overgeneralize from a few cases, so each should cite its source episodes and be reviewed or retired when evidence changes.

epimem.q: When is episodic memory the wrong tool?
epimem.model: When runs do not repeat, there is nothing to learn from. When failures are about current facts or session state, semantic or short-term memory is the fix. And once a routine is proven, store it as procedural memory rather than rereading episodes.

memwrite.q: What does honouring a DPDP erasure request involve for an AI assistant?
memwrite.model: Delete the personal data wherever the assistant holds it: rows, vector embeddings, rolling summaries and caches, with backups on their schedule. Keep records that other laws such as KYC or tax rules require in the system of record, not in agent memory, and log the erasure as proof. This is a summary, not legal advice.

memwrite.q: Design a write policy for a bank assistant’s long-term memory.
memwrite.model: Allow only named categories such as language, contact channel, goals and address; block OTPs, PAN, Aadhaar, card numbers and health data before any write; save only stable, reusable facts; let newer facts invalidate older ones with a date; and give one-off items a TTL.

memwrite.q: Hot-path or background memory writes: how do you choose?
memwrite.model: Writing in the hot path makes a fact available on the next turn but adds latency and cost to the user’s request. Writing in the background is cheaper and can consolidate better, but the fact appears later and the job must be scheduled and monitored.

memtools.q: How do you implement memory tool handlers safely?
memtools.model: Map each command onto per-tenant storage, resolve every path (including symlinks) before checking it is inside the memory root, reject anything that escapes, and log every write so it can be reviewed.

memtools.q: When would you choose a developer-run memory pipeline over agent-managed memory?
memtools.model: When writes must be predictable and auditable, as with regulated customer data. A pipeline with a fixed schema, filters and reconciliation is easier to test and review than an agent deciding what to store.

memtools.q: Explain the MemGPT idea in your own words.
pts: a small main context and larger stores
memtools.model: MemGPT treats the context window like an operating system treats RAM: a small main context backed by larger external stores. The agent calls functions to page information in and out, deciding itself what to keep in view.

procmem.q: In your own words: how is procedural memory different from simply keeping the agent’s past conversations?
pts: stores how-to procedures, not raw history
distilled and generalized from several runs
procmem.model: Past conversations are episodic memory: long, specific records of what happened. Procedural memory is distilled from several successful runs into a short, general procedure, such as a skill with steps and a check. It is retrieved only when a new task matches, so it keeps context small and tells the agent what to do rather than what once happened.

procmem.q: How would you choose the retrieval threshold for a skill library?
pts: wrong retrievals cost steps or errors
procmem.model: A low threshold loads the wrong procedure for unrelated tasks, which costs extra steps and can confuse the agent; a high one misses tasks that would have benefited. Label a sample of real tasks, sweep the threshold, and pick the one that minimizes total steps with no loss of correctness. Keep a verification step so a wrong retrieval is caught rather than shipped.

procmem.q: A skill that worked for months starts producing broken changes after a refactor. What should the system have done?
pts: track failures or the commit it was learned on
procmem.model: Each reuse should end with the skill’s check, so the first failure is caught instead of shipped. The skill should record the commit it was learned on and count failures; after repeated failures it is retired or revised, and the next run re-learns it. Skills are code-like assets, so changes to them deserve review.

graphmem.q: Explain temporal graph memory and when it beats vector memory.
graphmem.model: It stores entities and typed relationships, each with the time it was valid, and closes contradicted relationships with an end date. It beats vector memory when facts change and relate, such as nominees and addresses, and when questions chain facts or ask what was true at a date.

graphmem.q: 70% simple questions at 95% and 30% multi-hop at 85%. Overall accuracy?
The assistant tells a manager that Rahul is the nominee, but he was replaced last year. What went wrong and what do you change?
graphmem.model: The old nominee fact was never closed, so both nominees sat in memory without dates and the older one was retrieved. Store valid times, close contradicted edges when a change is recorded, answer from currently valid edges, and review extraction on samples.

cases.title: The assistant that remembered the address it was told to delete
cases.brief: A wealth platform's assistant advises investors across long sessions and comes back to the same customers for months. It holds the thread well enough that nobody noticed how it holds it: everything said stays in the window until the window runs out, every fact learned is appended, and nothing is ever removed. Compliance has now raised a DPDP erasure failure, and part of the team's answer is to buy a bigger context window.
evidence: Sessions average 140 turns. Answer quality drops measurably after about turn 60, and some sessions hit the context limit outright.
22% of investors who updated their risk profile were later advised on the old one, which is still in the store alongside the new.
An investor who requested DPDP erasure was greeted by name and old address on the next call. The rows were deleted; the vector index and a rolling summary still held them.
Part of the team wants to move to a 1M-token model so the assistant can “keep everything”. Nobody has measured where accuracy actually falls today.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.stm: Start here. 140 turns with nothing compacted is why quality falls off a cliff at 60 and why sessions die at the limit. Compact older turns into a running summary, keep the first message intact because it holds the task and the constraints, and never let a summary paraphrase an account number or an amount - carry those verbatim or by reference.
why.semmem: The old risk profile being advised on is an update failure, not a recall failure: the store appends, so both profiles are retrievable and the wrong one sometimes wins. Make a profile fact a single current value that updates in place, namespace every lookup by investor id, and test updates and “I don't know” rather than only recall.
why.memwrite: The erasure failure is the one with a regulator attached. Deleting rows while embeddings and a rolling summary keep the same data is the textbook half-deletion. Write a forget policy that reaches every copy - index, summaries, caches - run it as a tested job rather than a one-off script, and keep a deletion log of identifiers rather than of the deleted content.
why.ctxbudget: Useful, and it is the honest answer to the 1M-token proposal: measure where accuracy falls before buying more room. Curate what earns a place, drop near-duplicate and outdated chunks, and stop burying the most relevant material in the middle of a long prompt.
why.graphmem: Useful here and essential in Case 3: addresses and risk profiles are facts with validity periods, so dating them would also have prevented the old profile winning. Treat it as the deeper fix once the three above are in place.
why.epimem: Not needed on this evidence: nothing says the assistant repeats mistakes across runs or that past sessions predict the fix. The failures are about keeping the thread, updating a fact and deleting it, not about learning from its own history.
why.memtools: Not needed: the assistant is not running a multi-day task that must resume where it stopped, and letting it decide what to write to its own store is the last thing you want while the forget policy is broken.
why.procmem: Not needed: there is no repeated routine being performed differently each time. Procedural memory would be the answer if the assistant kept re-inventing a KYC re-verification, which is not what any symptom describes.

firstWhy.semmem: The right second step, and the one that costs the most trust - advising on a stale risk profile is a bad conversation to have. But at 140 turns with nothing compacted, a corrected fact can still be pushed out of the window before it is used, so the thread has to hold before the facts can be relied on.
firstWhy.memwrite: This has a regulator behind it, so the instinct to go first is reasonable, and it must be done this quarter. But the data you are trying to erase is being copied into rolling summaries by the compaction you have not designed yet - fix the thing generating copies, or you will write the forget policy twice.
firstWhy.ctxbudget: The right rebuttal to the 1M-token plan, and you should make that argument today. As an ordering choice, though, curating what goes in does not help a session that keeps nothing out, and at turn 120 the window fills regardless of how well each chunk was chosen.

cases.model: Start with short-term memory and compaction, because 140-turn sessions with nothing compacted explain both the quality cliff at turn 60 and the hard context failures: summarise older turns, keep the first message verbatim since it carries the task and the constraints, and copy identifiers and amounts exactly rather than letting a summary paraphrase them. Next, fix semantic memory so a profile fact has one current value that updates in place instead of accumulating, namespace every read by investor id, and evaluate updates and refusals rather than recall alone. Then write a real forget policy: erasure has to reach the vector index, the rolling summaries and any cache, run as a tested job with a deletion log that holds identifiers rather than the data itself. With those three in place, answer the 1M-token proposal with measurement - find where accuracy actually falls, drop outdated and near-duplicate chunks, and keep the most relevant material out of the middle of the prompt. Dating facts with validity periods is the deeper fix for the stale profile and is worth planning. Episodic, procedural and agent-managed memory address none of these four symptoms.
cases.note: Three of the four symptoms here are the same mistake wearing different clothes: nothing is ever replaced, only added. Case 3 takes that idea further - where facts have to change over time and an auditor asks what you knew in April - and Case 2 is about an agent that forgets everything instead, so do not carry one shape of memory failure forward as the shape.

stm: Symptom 1: 140 turns, quality falling away after 60, some sessions hitting the limit outright. Nothing is being removed from the window as the conversation grows. What manages the thread of a long session so it can keep going?

Not a bigger window. Something that condenses what has gone before into a form that still carries the thread - and that has to be careful about two things in particular: the first message, and any number.
Short-Term Memory and Compaction. Read all three pitfalls: the paraphrased amount, the dropped first message, and the cache invalidation from compacting a little every turn.
semmem: Symptom 2: 22% of investors who changed their risk profile were later advised on the old one, which is still sitting in the store next to the new one. The agent recalled successfully - it recalled the wrong thing. What kind of memory is this, and what is it doing wrong?

This is the store of what the agent knows about a person. The failure is not retrieval, it is that writing a new value did not retire the old one - and look at how lookups are scoped between users while you are there.
Semantic Memory. The first pitfall is this symptom exactly: an append-only store that keeps both the old and the new.
memwrite: Symptom 3: the rows were deleted, and the investor was still greeted with their old address, because it also lived in the vector index and a rolling summary. What has to be true for a deletion to actually be a deletion?
A policy about what gets saved and what must go, applied to every copy rather than the primary record, and run as a tested job rather than a script somebody remembers to execute.
Write and Forget Policies. Read the pitfall about deleting rows but leaving embeddings and summaries behind, and the note on what a deletion log should contain.

drop.epimem: Episodic memory helps an agent that keeps repeating the same mistakes across runs. Which symptom here is about a mistake being repeated, rather than a fact being stale, duplicated or undeleted?
drop.memtools: Letting the agent manage its own memory suits multi-day tasks that must resume where they stopped. Is that this workload - and what would self-directed writes do to the erasure problem?
drop.procmem: Procedural memory stores how a routine is done so it is not re-invented. Which symptom describes a routine the agent performs differently each time?

cases.firstHint: Your set is right. Now ask which of these the others are being undermined by: a corrected fact and a careful deletion are both pointless if the mechanism that holds the conversation is silently copying and then evicting whatever it likes.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A DPDP erasure has already failed, so the regulatory exposure is live and outranks quality problems.
Nothing is compacted across 140 turns, so what the agent holds - and what it copies - is unmanaged, and every other fix depends on that.
22% of updated risk profiles were advised on wrongly, which is the largest measured error rate on the page.
whyFirst.why: Order by what the other fixes are standing on. The erasure must happen and the stale profile is embarrassing, but both are being fed by an unmanaged window: compaction is what copies an address into a rolling summary you then have to erase, and eviction is what drops a corrected profile before it is used. Decide how the thread is kept, and the other two become fixes that stay fixed.

cases.title: The migration agent that starts over every morning
cases.brief: A platform team runs an agent through long database migrations: read the schema, write the transform, backfill in batches, verify counts, cut over. It is the fifteenth migration of this shape. The agent is competent within a session and has no idea it has ever done this before, and the engineer minding it has started keeping notes on paper.
evidence: The migration spans several days. After each nightly restart the agent re-derives its plan and redoes about two days of work, because progress exists only in the live session.

It repeats the same three mistakes every run - wrong null handling on the transform, backfilling before the index exists, re-applying a step already applied - and 40 transcripts of past runs sit unused.
This migration shape has been done 14 times with a stable sequence of tool calls. The agent re-invents the sequence each time, differently, and the engineer corrects it each time.
The agent's memory directory is guarded by a startswith path check. A test showed a path containing /memories/../ writing outside it.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.memtools: Start here, and it answers symptoms 1 and 4 together. Progress that lives only in the session is why two days of work is redone after every restart, so let the agent keep a progress file it writes often enough that a reset costs minutes rather than days. Fix the path check in the same change: startswith is not containment, and a store the agent can escape is worse than no store.
why.procmem: Fourteen runs of a stable sequence, re-invented differently each time, is the definition of a missing procedure. Record the sequence as a reviewed procedure the agent retrieves, so the fifteenth run follows the fourteenth instead of guessing - and review it, because an unreviewed procedure happily encodes last month's shortcut.
why.epimem: The same three mistakes every run, with 40 transcripts available, is history going unused. Store the lesson from each past run - not the transcript - and retrieve it when the situation matches, so null handling and backfill order come back as warnings rather than as rediscoveries.
why.stm: Useful: these are long sessions over large tool output, so compacting schema dumps and batch logs keeps the thread. Secondary, because the expensive loss here happens at the restart boundary, which compaction does not cross.
why.ctxbudget: Useful: schema dumps and verification logs are exactly the material that gets stuffed in whole. Worth curating once the agent stops redoing work, since right now the waste is measured in days rather than tokens.
why.semmem: Not needed: there is no user whose preferences and profile the agent should carry. The thing it must remember is its own work and its own procedure, which is a different store with different rules.
why.memwrite: Not needed on this evidence: no personal data is in play and no erasure obligation applies, so a forget policy has nothing to protect. Note how different that makes this module's answer from Case 1, where it was the item with a regulator attached.
why.graphmem: Not needed: nothing here is a relationship between entities changing over time, and no auditor is asking what was true on a given date. Schema facts are versioned by the migration itself.

firstWhy.procmem: This is the fix the engineer will thank you for, and it is second by a short head. But a recorded procedure still has to be executed across several days and nightly restarts, and today a restart throws away two days of it - so you would be replaying a perfect procedure from step one.
firstWhy.epimem: Right diagnosis of symptom 2, and the cheapest of the three to demonstrate since the 40 transcripts already exist. It makes each run smarter, though, while each run is still losing two days to a restart - so the lesson lands on work that gets thrown away.
firstWhy.stm: Reasonable: the sessions are long and the tool output is bulky, so this helps. But compaction manages memory within a session, and every expensive loss in this evidence happens at the moment a session ends.

cases.model: Start with agent-managed memory: give the agent a progress file it owns and writes often, so a nightly restart resumes where the work stopped instead of re-deriving the plan and redoing two days - and fix the containment check in the same change, because startswith is not a path check and /memories/../ is already escaping it. Next, capture the stable fourteen-run sequence as a reviewed procedure the agent retrieves rather than re-invents, with review as part of the process so an outdated step is not replayed with confidence. Then mine the 40 transcripts into episodic memory, storing the lesson from each run rather than the transcript, so null handling and backfill order return as warnings at the right moment. Add compaction for the long sessions and bulky schema and batch output, and curate what enters the window once the days of redone work have stopped. Semantic memory, forget policies and temporal graphs address nothing in this evidence: there is no user profile here, no personal data to erase, and no relationship changing over time.
cases.note: Case 1's assistant remembered things it should have dropped; this agent drops everything it should have kept, and the fix for a regulator there is irrelevant here. Decide which store is missing - the session, the user, the agent's own work, or the procedure - before choosing a technique.

memtools: Symptoms 1 and 4 both concern the same thing. Two days of work is redone after every restart because progress exists only in the live session, and the place the agent could write to is guarded by a check that does not hold. What lets an agent keep its own notes across a reset?
Hand the agent a store it writes to deliberately - progress, checklists, where it stopped - and then look very carefully at how that store is fenced off.
Agent-Managed Memory. The pitfall about checking the path with startswith is symptom 4 word for word, and the one about writing progress too rarely is symptom 1.
procmem: Symptom 3: this migration shape has been done 14 times with a stable sequence of tool calls, and the agent invents a different sequence every time while an engineer corrects it. What kind of memory holds how a routine is done?
Not what happened once, and not what the user likes - the repeatable method itself, retrieved when the same kind of task comes round again. Pay attention to who checks it before it is trusted.
Procedural Memory. Read the pitfalls about stale procedures replaying outdated steps and unreviewed memories storing shortcuts.
epimem: Symptom 2: the same three mistakes on every run, and 40 transcripts of past runs sitting unused. What kind of memory answers “have I been here before?”
Recall of specific past episodes, retrieved when the situation resembles them - and the thing you store is not the whole run.
Episodic Memory. Note the pitfall about injecting whole transcripts instead of the lesson they teach, which is the trap with 40 of them available.

drop.semmem: Semantic memory holds what the agent knows about a person across weeks. Who is the person in this case, and what preference of theirs is being forgotten?
drop.memwrite: Forget policies exist to make deletion real and to keep stores from holding what they should not. What personal data is in a database migration, and who has asked for it to be erased?
drop.graphmem: Temporal graph memory answers who was linked to what, and since when. Which fact in this evidence changes over time in a way an auditor would ask about?

cases.firstHint: Your three are right and they reinforce each other. Now ask where the loss actually happens: two of them make a run smarter, and one of them decides whether the run survives the night.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A path check that /memories/../ can escape is a security hole, and security always goes first.
The agent re-invents a 14-time-proven sequence, which is the largest and most repeated waste of the engineer's time.
Everything the other fixes produce is lost at the nightly restart, so durable progress is what makes them worth having.
whyFirst.why: Order by what survives. A retrieved procedure and a learned lesson both improve the work in progress, and the restart boundary throws that work away twice a week - so they pay off properly only once progress is durable. The path check is urgent, but it is part of the same change rather than a separate first step: you are fixing the store the agent is about to start relying on.

cases.title: The nominee question that gets a different answer each time
cases.brief: A life insurer's servicing assistant answers questions about policies, nominees, addresses and authorised signatories, for staff and for customers. Calls are short - six turns on average - so nobody has worried about session length. What people have worried about is that the same question can get two different answers on two days, and that an auditor's request for what the insurer knew on a given date went unanswered for three weeks.
evidence: Asked who the nominee is on the policy opened after the customer moved to Pune, the assistant answers differently on different days. Both cities are stored, neither has a date.
Addresses, nominees and authorised signatories all change over the life of a policy. The store appends every version, so “what did we know on 1 April?” cannot be answered at all.
A customer's date of birth was corrected in March. 31% of answers since then have used the old one, retrieved from an older note that was never retired.
Erasure requests delete the policy rows and leave the embeddings and a monthly rolling summary untouched.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.graphmem: Start here, because symptoms 1 and 2 are one fault and it is the fault this whole module builds towards. A question like “the nominee on the policy opened after the move” chains facts and depends on when each was true; storing both cities with no dates makes the answer a coin toss. Give every fact a validity period and keep the superseded version rather than deleting it, so the chain resolves and the auditor's date question becomes a query.
why.semmem: The stale date of birth is the update half of the same disease: a correction was written and the old note was never retired, so both are retrievable and the wrong one wins 31% of the time. A profile fact needs one current value, updated in place, with lookups namespaced by customer, and the tests have to cover updates rather than only recall.
why.memwrite: Deleting policy rows while embeddings and a monthly summary keep the same personal data is a half-deletion with a regulator attached. The forget policy has to reach every copy, run as a tested job, and log identifiers rather than content - and it has to coexist with dated history, which is the interesting part: retention and erasure are both requirements here.
why.ctxbudget: Useful: once facts are dated, the right few retrieved facts replace the broad note-dump the assistant reads now, and near-duplicate versions stop acting as distractors.
why.procmem: Useful: servicing has repeated routines - a nominee change, an address update - worth storing as reviewed procedures so each is performed the same way. Secondary to making the facts themselves trustworthy.
why.stm: Not needed, and worth noticing: calls average six turns, so there is nothing to compact and no window pressure. This is the same module as Case 1, where 140-turn sessions made compaction the first move - the technique did not change, the workload did.
why.epimem: Not needed: nothing says the assistant repeats mistakes across runs. Its errors come from the facts it holds, not from failing to learn from its own history.
why.memtools: Not needed: a six-turn servicing call is not a multi-day task resuming where it stopped, and letting the assistant write to its own store while the forget policy leaks is the wrong order of operations.

firstWhy.semmem: Close, and the two are nearly the same fix seen at different depths - this is the strongest wrong answer on the page. But current-value semantics alone cannot answer symptom 1: “the policy opened after the move” needs to know when the old address stopped being true, and a single current value has thrown that away.
firstWhy.memwrite: There is a regulator behind this and it must ship. But erasure and dated history have to be designed together - a forget policy written against today's undated append-only store will be rewritten the moment facts get validity periods, and you will have deleted the audit trail you were about to need.
firstWhy.ctxbudget: Curating what the assistant reads would genuinely reduce the distractors. But the two versions of the address are both legitimately in the store today, so no amount of careful selection tells you which one was true in April.

cases.model: Start with graph and temporal memory, because the flipping nominee answer and the unanswerable audit question are the same gap: facts here change over the life of a policy and none of them carries a date. Model addresses, nominees and signatories as dated relationships with validity periods, supersede rather than delete, and the chained question - the nominee on the policy opened after the move - resolves deterministically while “what did we know on 1 April” becomes an ordinary query. Next fix semantic memory so a corrected fact retires the old one: one current value per profile fact, updated in place, namespaced by customer, with updates and refusals in the test set rather than recall alone. Then write a forget policy that reaches the embeddings and the rolling summary as well as the rows, runs as a tested job, and logs identifiers rather than content - designed alongside the dated history, since this domain owes both retention and erasure. With trustworthy facts, curate what actually enters the window, and store the common servicing routines as reviewed procedures. Compaction, episodic memory and agent-managed memory have nothing to do here: calls are six turns long, the assistant is not repeating its own mistakes, and no task spans days.
cases.note: Across the three cases the memory that was missing was different each time - the session, the agent's own work, the dated fact - and compaction went from the first move in Case 1 to not needed here on the strength of one number: turns per session. Read the workload before reaching for a store.

graphmem: Read symptoms 1 and 2 together. “The policy opened after the customer moved to Pune” needs two facts and their order in time, both cities are stored with no dates, and nobody can say what was known on 1 April. What is missing from every fact in this store?
Facts here are relationships between things, and they were true for a period rather than forever. Add that period and the chained question and the audit question answer themselves.
Graph and Temporal Memory. All three pitfalls are in this evidence: losing the audit trail by deleting, keeping contradictions with no dates, and unreviewed wrong edges.
semmem: Symptom 3: a date of birth was corrected in March, and 31% of answers since have used the old one from a note nobody retired. The retrieval worked - what did the write fail to do?
This is the store of what is known about a person. Writing a new value has to retire the old one rather than sit beside it, and what you test has to include the update, not just the recall.
Semantic Memory. The first pitfall - an append-only store keeping both the old and the new - is this symptom, and the third explains why nobody caught it.
memwrite: Symptom 4: policy rows are deleted and the embeddings and a monthly rolling summary keep the same personal data. What has to be true for an erasure to be an erasure - and how does that sit alongside an auditor who needs history kept?
A policy for what is saved and what must go, applied to every copy rather than the primary record, run as a tested job - and here it has to coexist with deliberately retained dated history.
Write and Forget Policies. Read the pitfall about embeddings and summaries surviving a row delete, and the note on what the deletion log should contain.

drop.stm: Compaction manages a conversation that has grown too long to hold. How many turns does a servicing call run to here - and what would there be to compact?
drop.epimem: Episodic memory stops an agent repeating its own past mistakes. Are these errors mistakes the assistant made before, or facts it is holding wrongly right now?
drop.memtools: Agent-managed memory suits a multi-day task that must resume where it stopped. Which task in this case spans more than one call?

cases.firstHint: You have the right three, and two of them are closer together than they look. Ask what symptom 1 actually requires: not the current value of the address, but knowing when the old one stopped being true - and only one of your techniques stores that.

whyFirst.q: Before you check - which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: A stale date of birth is used in 31% of answers, the largest measured error rate here.
Two of the four symptoms need to know when a fact stopped being true, which no current-value store can answer.
An erasure request is leaving personal data in the embeddings, which carries regulatory exposure.
whyFirst.why: Order by what the questions actually require. Retiring stale values fixes the 31% and must happen; erasure must happen too. But a single current value cannot answer “the policy opened after the move” or “what did we know on 1 April”, and a forget policy written before the history is dated will delete the trail the auditor wants. Decide how time is represented first, and the other two are built on something that holds.

ctxbudget.t: An agent sends 60 clauses of 1,500 tokens each plus a 500-token question on every call. You keep the top 5 clauses instead. By what percentage do input tokens fall?
iv: Why not just use the model with the biggest context window?

Advertised length is not effective length: accuracy falls as input grows even on simple tasks, distractors hurt more at long lengths, and facts in the middle are used worst. A bigger window also costs more per call. Curate first, then measure accuracy at your real lengths.
How do you choose what goes into the window?

Inventory tokens per segment, rank candidate chunks by relevance, keep the top ones until an effective budget found by your own eval, place documents first and the question last, and load everything else just in time through tools.
mis: Sizing the prompt to the advertised maximum
Measure where your own eval accuracy drops and budget below it
Placing the key chunk in the middle of a long prompt
Put the most relevant material at the start and the question at the end

stm.t: A session has 40 tool results of 3,500 tokens each. Clearing keeps the last 3 results. How many tokens of tool results are cleared?
iv: What is the difference between clearing tool results and compaction?

Clearing removes old tool outputs, which can be re-fetched, and keeps the call record; it is one of the safest reductions. Compaction summarizes the conversation itself, so it needs instructions that keep IDs, amounts, decisions and open tasks.
Why clear in large steps rather than a little every turn?
Every change to earlier content invalidates the prompt cache from that point. Clearing at least a large amount at a time (clear_at_least) means fewer cache rewrites for the same saving.
mis: Letting the summary paraphrase account numbers and amounts
Instruct the summary to copy identifiers, amounts and open tasks verbatim
Dropping the oldest message first
Pin the task and constraints; compact the middle

semmem.t: Replaying full history costs 26,000 tokens per turn. Retrieving 3 facts costs 180 tokens. What percentage of those tokens does retrieval save?
iv: How do you keep user facts current?

Reconcile each new candidate fact with the most similar stored facts and choose add, update, delete or no-op, or keep validity windows and invalidate the old fact. Test with questions whose answer changed over time.
How do you stop one user’s memories reaching another?
Namespace every write and search by tenant and user ID, enforce it in the storage layer rather than in the prompt, and test cross-user queries in CI.
mis: An append-only store that keeps both the old and the new address
Reconcile updates, or invalidate the older fact with a date
Evaluating only recall of facts
Also test updates, time questions and abstention

epimem.t: Recency decays by 0.995 per hour. What is the recency of an episode that is 100 hours old? Give it to two decimals.
iv: How does an agent choose which past episodes to recall?

Score each episode on recency (exponential decay), importance (rated when written) and relevance (similarity to the current situation), normalize each score, weight and add them, and take the top few.
What does reflection add to episodic memory?
It condenses many related episodes into a short, cited lesson, so the agent injects one line of guidance instead of several transcripts, saving tokens and generalizing better.
mis: Adding raw scores on different scales
Min-max normalize each component before weighting
Injecting whole past transcripts
Inject short lessons that cite their source episodes

memwrite.t: A user’s data sits in 4 table rows, 4 vectors, 1 rolling summary and 1 cache entry. Deletion removes only the table rows. What fraction of the copies survive, as a percentage?
iv: What should never go into an assistant’s long-term memory?

OTPs, passwords, card numbers, Aadhaar and PAN, and health details, unless there is a clear lawful purpose and controls. Save only allow-listed, stable, reusable categories, and filter before writing.
What does honouring an erasure request involve for an AI assistant?

Deleting every copy of the personal data it holds: rows, embeddings, summaries, caches and backups on their schedule, while keeping records other laws require in the system of record, and logging the erasure.
mis: Deleting table rows but not embeddings or summaries
Track every derived copy and delete them together
Saving everything and filtering at read time
Filter and classify before anything is written

memtools.t: Without memory, each of 3 sessions re-reads everything: 160k tokens each. With memory, session 1 costs 90k and sessions 2 and 3 cost 60k each. What percentage of tokens is saved?
iv: Why is a startswith check not enough for memory paths?
A path like /memories/../secrets.txt starts with /memories but resolves outside it. Resolve the full path first, including symlinks, then check that it stays inside the memory root.
When would you not give the agent memory tools?

When writes must be predictable and auditable, as in regulated customer data. A developer-run pipeline with a fixed schema and policy is easier to test and review than an agent deciding what to store.
mis: Validating paths with a string prefix
Resolve, then check the root; reject symlinks out
Letting the agent write without logs
Log every write and review a sample

procmem.t: Without a skill a task takes 9 steps; with it, 4. The task runs 20 times a month at about 3k tokens per step. How many tokens does the skill save per month, in thousands?
procmem.a: (9 − 4) steps × 3k tokens × 20 runs = 300k tokens a month, plus fewer chances to go wrong.
iv: What's the difference between procedural, semantic and episodic memory for agents?

Procedural memory stores how to do things (workflows, skills). Semantic memory stores facts (codebase conventions, domain knowledge). Episodic memory stores specific past runs. Procedural mostly cuts steps; semantic cuts lookups.
How do you keep procedural memories from going stale?
Tie each procedure to tests or checks, record its source and date, re-validate it when related code changes, and retire procedures that start failing.
mis: Saving every trajectory as memory
Save only repeated, successful, reviewed procedures
Skills with no verification step
End every skill with a check such as tests passing

graphmem.t: 70% of questions are simple (95% correct) and 30% multi-hop (85% correct). What is overall accuracy, in percent?
iv: When would you use a temporal knowledge graph for agent memory?

When facts relate to each other and change over time, such as nominees, addresses and account holders, and when questions chain facts or ask what was true at a date. Close old edges with end dates rather than deleting.
What is the difference between valid time and recorded time?
Valid time is when a fact was true in the world; recorded time is when the system learned it. Keeping both lets you answer what was true then and what we knew then.
mis: Deleting superseded facts
Close them with an end date
Using vector memory for chained questions
Store relationships and traverse them

gloss: context window
The maximum number of tokens a model can consider in one request, including the prompt and its output.
context engineering
Choosing and arranging the tokens a model sees at each step: instructions, memories, history and tool results.
context rot
The drop in accuracy as input length grows, even when the task itself stays simple.
lost in the middle
The finding that models use information at the start or end of a long input better than information in the middle.
effective context
The input length at which a model still performs well on your task, often far below the advertised maximum.
compaction
Summarizing older parts of a conversation into a shorter block so the session can continue within the window.
tool-result clearing
Removing old tool outputs from the context while keeping the record that the call happened.
checkpointer
A component that saves an agent’s thread state by session ID so it can resume later.
semantic memory
Durable facts about users or entities kept outside the model and retrieved when relevant.
episodic memory
Records of specific past runs or experiences, retrieved when a similar situation comes up.
reflection
Condensing several episodes into a short, higher-level lesson that cites them.
namespace
A key prefix, such as tenant and user ID, that scopes where memories are written and searched.
TTL
Time to live: how long an item is kept before it expires automatically.
DPDP Act
India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which includes duties to erase personal data on request or when its purpose ends.
path traversal
Using sequences such as ../ to reach files outside an allowed directory.
temporal knowledge graph
A graph of entities and relationships where each relationship carries the time it was valid.
edge invalidation
Marking a relationship as no longer true by setting its end date, instead of deleting it.

procmem.name: Prompt & Tool Controls
procmem.note: Reusing a proven procedure cuts steps, the biggest driver of agent token spend.

procmem.name: Episodic Memory
procmem.note: Episodes record what happened; procedural memory keeps the tested routine distilled from them.

procmem.name: Shared State vs Message Passing
procmem.note: Procedural memory is one agent’s store; shared state is about concurrent writes and read scopes across several agents.

procmem.name: Agent Skills
procmem.note: Skills are hand-written procedures; procedural memory is procedures the agent learns and saves itself.

ctxbudget.name: Context Pruning
ctxbudget.note: Pruning cuts tokens to save money; context budgeting curates and orders them so accuracy holds at length.

ctxbudget.name: Prefix Caching
ctxbudget.note: Put stable content first so it can be cached, and the question last so it is used best.

ctxbudget.name: Tool Search and Large Tool Sets
ctxbudget.note: Tool definitions are part of the context budget; deferring most of them frees room for history and retrieved facts.

ctxbudget.name: Parallel Sub-Agents with Isolated Context
ctxbudget.note: Isolating each piece in its own sub-agent and returning a 500-token card is a context budget enforced by architecture.

ctxbudget.name: Long-Context Prompting
ctxbudget.note: A long document prefix eats the context budget; decide what stays in context and what is retrieved.

stm.name: Context Pruning
stm.note: Compaction is pruning with a rule about what must survive: IDs, amounts, decisions and open tasks.

stm.name: Prompt Caching
stm.note: Every clear or compaction rewrites the prompt prefix, so clear in fewer, larger steps to protect the cache.

semmem.name: Hybrid Search
semmem.note: Memory search runs on the same retrieval stack: hybrid search over a per-user namespace.

semmem.name: Graph and Temporal Memory
semmem.note: Semantic memory stores facts; a temporal graph adds the links between them and when each was true.

epimem.name: Procedural Memory
epimem.note: Episodes record what happened; procedural memory keeps the tested routine distilled from them.

memwrite.name: PII Detection and Redaction
memwrite.note: The same PII redaction that screens prompts should screen what is written to memory.

memwrite.name: Indirect Prompt Injection
memwrite.note: Injected text written to long-term memory keeps attacking future sessions; memory write policies are a defence.

memwrite.name: India’s DPDP Act and Rules
memwrite.note: A DPDP erasure request must reach agent memory and embeddings, not just the main database.

memwrite.name: Graph and Temporal Memory
memwrite.note: Closing contradicted edges with an end date is a write policy; erasure requests still remove the person entirely.

memtools.name: Action Policies and Approval Thresholds
memtools.note: Memory tools need least privilege: a fixed root, resolved paths and logged writes.

graphmem.name: Semantic Memory
graphmem.note: Semantic memory stores facts; a temporal graph adds the links between them and when each was true.

graphmem.name: Write and Forget Policies
graphmem.note: Closing contradicted edges with an end date is a write policy; erasure requests still remove the person entirely.

graphmem.name: Audit Trails and Explainability
graphmem.note: Valid and recorded times let you show what the system knew at the time of a decision.

gifs.ctxbudget: A 14k-token prompt keeps only the top six chunks with the key fact first and the question last, raising illustrative accuracy from 58% to 86% at the same size.
gifs.epimem: Past episodes are ranked by recency, importance and relevance, and a reflection turns five episodes into one short lesson about a timing-out API.
gifs.graphmem: A temporal knowledge graph links Priya to account 4471 as holder since 2019, Rahul as nominee from March 2024 to June 2025, and an old Pune address that ended in January 2025. Contradicted facts get an end date instead of being deleted. Multi-hop answers rise from 45 percent with vector memory to 85 percent, and stale facts returned fall from 16 to 1 in 100 queries.
gifs.memtools: An agent writes its progress to a memory file, resumes from it in the next session, is blocked from path traversal, and finishes in 210k tokens instead of 480k.
gifs.memwrite: A write policy saves five of ten candidate memories, blocks OTP and PAN, invalidates an old address, and an erasure request removes every copy while one audit line stays.
gifs.procmem: A first run explores an endpoint task in 9 steps and saves the routine as a skill; a similar task retrieves it at similarity 0.88 and finishes in 4 checked steps, cutting tokens from 27k to 12k.
gifs.semmem: An agent stores three facts about an investor, updates the city when it changes, and sends 180 tokens of facts instead of 26,000 tokens of history.
gifs.stm: Context grows each turn until it crosses a 150k trigger; old tool results are cleared and history is compacted to a 6k summary that still keeps all five early facts.

header.lede: An agent knows only what is in its context window right now, so every long-running agent needs a policy for what goes in, what gets summarized, what is saved, which proven routines are reused, and what is forgotten.
